title: Value: NPV by start year and risk reduction

blocks.text: 14.2.4 Value: NPV by Start Year and Risk Reduction
Finance and the asset team both had comments on the step-03 plan:

Finance: you value every project at its earliest-start NPV, whatever year you start it. A project started in 2030 is worth less than the same project started in 2027; we sent you the NPV for every start year. Use it.
Asset management: NPV is not why we replace old equipment. Each project lowers the failure risk of one asset. We want to see how much risk a plan removes, and a plan that removes the most of it.
The Step-03 Plan Claims Value Its Starts Don't Have
`value_by_start.py` takes the step-03 plan of GridCap small (a fictional utility) and prices each funded project at finance's NPV for the year it actually starts:
step 03 plan: claims $26,108k; its starts are worth $23,909k (11 projects start after their earliest year)

The model claimed $2,199k that the plan does not have. The lesson *Many years: start years, windows and cash-flow spreading* left this gap open: $`v_i`$ did not depend on $`t`$, so a late start cost the model nothing and eleven projects drifted late. The code cannot do better because `Project` keeps one number, `value`, and the export's NPV by year is never read. Risk is not in the code at all.
A Coefficient per Variable Prices Each Start Year

The model already has one variable per project and start year, so the fix is a coefficient per variable: $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ from finance (lesson 7.2.4) on $`x_{i,t}`$. Risk gets the same shape: $`r_{i,t}`$, the risk a start in year $`t`$ removes. Both are computed before the model is built, in a new file, because they are data about projects, not rows.
For $`r_{i,t}`$ the design question was where risk comes from:

rows: a risk score column in the export
someone else's formula, untestable here; the asset team would have to rerun it for every start year
the asset's predicted RUL as a hard deadline
a deadline throws away how fast risk grows (lesson 7.3.2)
PoF from the asset's Weibull curve times CoF, summed over the years after the work (chosen)
every number traceable to the export's asset columns; lessons 7.3.1 to 7.3.4
a formula the planner owns and must test

blocks.text: The annual probability of failure (PoF) of an asset aged $`a`$ at the start of a year, given it has not failed yet, from its Weibull shape $`\beta`$ and scale $`\eta`$ (lesson 7.3.1):
\text{pof}(a) = 1 - \exp\!\left( \left(\tfrac{a}{\eta}\right)^{\beta} - \left(\tfrac{a+1}{\eta}\right)^{\beta} \right)

Its risk in year $`y`$ is $`\text{pof}(a_0 + y - y_0) \times \text{CoF}`$, with $`a_0`$ the asset's age in the plan's first year $`y_0`$ (the export's `age` column, read as `Asset.age`) and CoF its consequence of failure in $k (lesson 7.3.3). A start in $`t`$ finishes the work at the end of year $`t + d_i - 1`$, so it removes the risk of every year from $`t + d_i`$ to the plan's last year (lesson 7.3.4). Risk after the plan's last year is not counted: the planner compares plans over the same years.
For P022, a three-year tower set repair on a 35-year-old asset:

P022 (A022, age 35, beta 3.56, eta 49.1, CoF $458k), 3 years of work:
  start 2027: NPV $1,496k, risk removed $36.1k  (PoF 2030: 0.038, 2031: 0.041)
  start 2028: NPV $1,287k, risk removed $18.6k  (PoF 2031: 0.041)
  start 2029: NPV $1,102k, risk removed $0.0k  (PoF no year left in the plan)

A 2029 start finishes in 2031 and leaves no year inside the plan to remove risk from. NPV and risk both fall with a later start, but not in the same proportion, and that difference is what the next lesson trades.
The Model

The model of the lesson *Business rules: must-dos, bundles, parents and alternatives*, with the objective changed. The planners choose which measure to maximize with a setting in the request, `objective`, "npv" (the default) or "risk".
**Sets.** $`P`$, $`Y`$, $`T_i`$, $`M`$, $`\mathcal{G}`$, $`\mathcal{B}`$, $`C`$ as in the lesson *Business rules: must-dos, bundles, parents and alternatives*.

**Parameters.** $`c_{i,k}`$, $`B_y`$ as before ($k); $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ started in $`t`$ ($k), from the export; $`r_{i,t}`$, the risk it removes, computed as above ($k); $`L_c`$, the lags.
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$.
**Objective.** One of
**Constraints.** Unchanged:

\begin{aligned}
\text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in g} \text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\text{started}(j) - \text{started}(b_1) &= 0 && \forall B \in \mathcal{B},\ j \in B \setminus \{b_1\} && \text{(bundle}_{b_1,j}) \\
\text{started\_by}(c, t) - \text{started\_by}(p(c), t - L_c) &\le 0 && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\; t \le y < t + d_i} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}
Whatever is maximized, the plan's NPV and risk are both reported.
The Change, File by File
**`cipt/value.py`.** Before: the stub of the lesson *Business rules: must-dos, bundles, parents and alternatives*, every function returning 0.0. After, from `steps/04/cipt/value.py`:
<!-- snapshot: steps/04/cipt/value.py -->

The rest of `value.py` turns that curve into the coefficient $`r_{i,t}`$ of every start, and the page leaves its code to the practice. Three functions, each one step of the section *A Coefficient per Variable Prices Each Start Year* above:

items: `annual_risk(request, project, year)` is the risk of the project's asset in one calendar year if nothing is done: $`\text{pof}(a_0 + y - y_0) \times \text{CoF}`$, in $k. The asset is `project.asset` (the `Asset` record below), $`a_0`$ is its `age` and $`y_0`$ is the plan's first year, `request.years[0]`.

`risk_reduction(request, project, start)` is $`r_{i,t}`$, and its docstring says what it counts: "Risk removed by a start in `start`: every year after the work ends, to the plan's last year." That is the annual risks of every year from $`t + d_i`$ to the plan's last year, `request.years[-1]`, added up. A start whose work ends in the plan's last year removes no risk inside the plan, so it is 0.0.

`coefficients(request)` prices every start before the model is built: a dict whose key is `(project_id, t)` for every project and every `t` in `request.starts(p)`, and whose value is the pair ($`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, $`r_{i,t}`$), with the NPV read from `p.npv[t]`.

blocks.text: `coefficients` is keyed exactly like `built.x`, so the model can zip them without a lookup that might miss.

**`cipt/data.py`.** A new `Asset` record (`age`, `weibull_beta`, `weibull_eta`, `cof`); `Project` replaces the field `value` with `npv`, a dict by start year, and an `asset`. `value` survives as a property, the earliest-start NPV, because the tests of the lesson *The first request: fund projects within one budget* read it. From `steps/04/cipt/data.py`:
<!-- snapshot: steps/04/cipt/data.py -->
`Request` gains `objective`; the loader refuses any value but "npv" and "risk", so a typo in a planner's setting fails at load time instead of maximizing the wrong thing.
**`cipt/model.py`.** `Built` keeps both measures as expressions, and the objective picks one. From `steps/04/cipt/model.py`:
<!-- snapshot: steps/04/cipt/model.py -->

value = coefficients(request)
    built.npv = mathopt.fast_sum(value[key][0] * v for key, v in x.items())
    built.risk = mathopt.fast_sum(value[key][1] * v for key, v in x.items())
    model.maximize(built.npv if request.objective == "npv" else built.risk)
Keeping both on `Built` is what the next lesson needs: a second goal is then one row on an expression that already exists.

**`cipt/solve.py` and `cipt/plan.py`.** `Plan` gains `npv` and `risk`, and `read_plan` evaluates both expressions at the solution. `LinearSum` has no `evaluate` method; MathOpt's `evaluate_expression` does the work. From `steps/04/cipt/solve.py`:
<!-- snapshot: steps/04/cipt/solve.py -->

**`cipt/report.py`.** Three changes. The funded line's `value` is now the plan's objective, what the model maximized: the NPV of the actual starts when the objective is "npv", the risk removed when it is "risk". A new line after it gives both measures. And each project line's column label changes from `value` to `npv`, with the NPV of the year the project actually starts instead of the earliest-start value. **`cipt/goals.py`** is new and is the stub for the lesson *Two goals: risk against NPV*. No code of this step imports it, and in this lesson's practice it is already this stub.
Maximizing NPV and Maximizing Risk Give Different Plans

maximize npv : NPV $ 24,260k, risk removed $3,709.1k, 27 projects funded
maximize risk: NPV $ 18,559k, risk removed $6,827.9k, 31 projects funded

The NPV plan is worth $351k more than the step-03 plan's starts were ($23,909k), with the same rules and budgets: starting the right projects early is worth money the old objective could not see. The risk plan removes 84% more risk and gives up $5,701k of NPV. It funds four more projects within the same budgets. Neither plan is wrong; they answer different questions, and the planners asked both.
On the demo export, the report now shows NPV for each actual start: P001 starts in 2029 and is worth $1,077k there, not the $1,386k the earlier steps printed.

$ python -m cipt data/demo.json    # steps/04
GridCap tiny: optimal
funded 5 of 8 projects, capex $6,000k of $7,890k, value $2,473k
NPV $2,473k, risk reduced $740.3k (maximized: npv)
A Formula Gets a Test With a Value You Can Compute by Hand

With $`\beta = 1`$ the Weibull curve is the exponential distribution, which has no memory: every year's PoF is $`1 - e^{-1/\eta}`$ whatever the age. The tests use that to pin the formula to a number a reader can check. From `steps/04/tests/test_value.py`:
<!-- snapshot: steps/04/tests/test_value.py -->

def test_risk_reduction_counts_the_years_after_the_work():
    request = load_request(export([row("A", (100,), 50, latest=2028, asset=FLAT)], years=THREE))
    a, yearly = request.project("A"), 1000 * (1 - math.exp(-0.1))
    assert value.risk_reduction(request, a, 2027) == pytest.approx(2 * yearly)
    assert value.risk_reduction(request, a, 2028) == pytest.approx(yearly)

Value Added a File, Not Branches

14.2.4: steps/03 -> steps/04
  package lines 265 -> 324, functions 27 -> 31, tests 22 -> 28
  most branches: data.load_request (8) -> data.load_request (10)
  data.py        85 ->  105
  goals.py        0 ->   13
  model.py       38 ->   44
  plan.py        15 ->   18
  report.py      24 ->   25
  solve.py       34 ->   36
  value.py        9 ->   23

The change touched six files but `value.py` holds all of the arithmetic, in four functions that take plain values and return numbers. `model.py` grew by six lines and has no formula in it. The loader is again the most-branched function: every new column is read and checked there.

**Practice.** This lesson's project practice starts from `steps/03`, the whole package. It is graded by the tests in the practice's `tests/` folder and by a check that `main.py`, which plans the demo export, prints what the practice's `expected/report.txt` holds.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Summary

items: **The step-03 plan claims value its starts don't have**: $26,108k claimed, $23,909k real.
**A coefficient per variable prices each start year**: $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ and $`r_{i,t}`$ on $`x_{i,t}`$, both computed in `value.py` before the model is built.
**Risk removed is PoF times CoF over the years after the work**, from the asset's Weibull curve.
**Maximizing NPV and maximizing risk give different plans**: $24,260k and $3,709k against $18,559k and $6,828k.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: CoF times the PoF at the asset's age in year $`y`$
$`r_{i,t}`$: risk of years $`t + d_i`$ to the plan's last

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt `expressions.py` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/expressions.py) (`evaluate_expression`, used to read both measures at the solution); [MathOpt `model.py` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/model.py) (`Model.maximize` sets the objective to the expression it is given, which is how one model serves either goal).
Challenges

items: P022's risk removed is $36.1k for a 2027 start. Compute the 2030 term by hand from the formula and the printed PoF.
Count risk after the plan's last year, for ten more years, and predict how the risk plan changes. Which lesson of section 7 discusses the horizon?
Write a test that fails if `risk_reduction` counted the last year of work itself.

blocks.text: Design Note: Keep Both Measures on `Built`

The model maximizes one measure, but `Built` holds both, and every plan reports both. A plan that reports only what it maximized hides what it gave up: the risk plan's $5,701k of NPV would be invisible. Holding both expressions also makes the next lesson cheap, since a frontier only adds a row on one of them and maximizes the other.
The Full Programs

**value_by_start.py.** Prices the step-03 plan at the NPV of its real starts, prints P022's NPV, PoF and risk for each start year, and solves with each objective using `steps/04`. *Try:* print the five projects with the most risk removed per $k of capex, and predict whether the risk plan funds them all.
**cli_demo.py, ledger.py, code_size.py.** The demo run, the test ledger and the size table for step 04.
